Summarise each taxon's trait values: observed means and most frequent values

Source: R/summarise_trait_means.R
summarise_trait_means.Rd

One row per taxon and trait, computed directly from the records, with no model: for a numeric trait, the observed mean, a geometric mean, or an arithmetic mean for a trait on a signed scale; for a categorical trait, the most frequent value and the count of every value. Works on a whole database, on any subset of one made with the extract_*() functions (the taxa of one family, the records from one state), and on a table made by flatten_database().

Usage

summarise_trait_means(
  database,
  traits = NULL,
  by = NULL,
  collapse_to_species = TRUE,
  value_type_rules = NULL
)

Arguments

database

a traits.build database (a list of tables), or a flat table from one: a table made by flatten_database(), or a traits table.

traits

names of the traits to summarise. The default, NULL, is every trait in database. A trait named here that has no records gives a warning.

by

names of further variables to group by, as well as taxon and trait: columns of the traits table or, when database is the relational database, context properties. The default, NULL, is none.

collapse_to_species

logical: count the records of subspecies, varieties and forms towards their species? Default TRUE.

value_type_rules

a data frame with columns dataset_id and value_type, one row per value type to use from a dataset in place of the default raw, mean and median, for a dataset that reports numeric values another way. For example, a dataset of specimen labels that gives one bound per specimen and no raw values would have a row for minimum and one for maximum, each bound then counting as an observation. The default, NULL, is no such datasets.

Value

A tibble with one row per taxon, by group and trait (and unit, for a numeric trait), ordered by those. trait_means_dictionary() defines its columns. The taxon columns (taxon_rank, genus, family, establishment_means, taxon_id) are those the database's taxa table has.

Details

Numeric traits. Records are first summarised in groups, and the taxon's value is the mean of the groups, each counting once whatever its number of records, so a study that measured many individuals at one site counts once for that site.

  • Records with value_type raw, mean or median are grouped by dataset and location. They are used whatever their basis of record or life stage.

  • Minimum and maximum records whose basis_of_record is preserved_specimen or literature (floras) are grouped by observation; a flora's range gives one midpoint. Other minimum and maximum records are not used.

  • A dataset named in value_type_rules contributes the value types given there instead, grouped by dataset and location.

Everything is done on the log scale: a group's value is the geometric mean of its records (for a flora range, the geometric midpoint, sqrt(minimum * maximum), or the lone bound if only one is given), and value is the geometric mean of the groups. Traits are treated as log-normal, for which the geometric mean is the median. A geometric mean needs positive values, so records with a zero or negative value are not used. The arithmetic mean of the same groups is given alongside, in arithmetic_mean.

Signed traits. A trait whose values can be negative, such as a water potential, a temperature or an isotope ratio, is not log-normal and has no geometric mean. For such a trait value is the arithmetic mean of the same groups (a flora range gives its arithmetic midpoint), every record is used, including zeros and negative values, method is "arithmetic", and log_value and sd_log are empty. A trait is signed when its definition allows values below zero (allowed_values_min in the database's definitions). A flat table carries no definitions, so there a trait is signed when any of its records is negative; summarise the relational database to have the definitions decide, so that a subset whose records all happen to be positive is treated as the whole database is.

Categorical traits. A record listing several space-separated values counts once for each. value_mode is the most frequent value, with tied values joined by a space, and value_count lists every value with its count, and method is "mode".

Months. A trait that records the months of something, such as flowering_time or fruiting_time, holds a twelve-letter string of y and n per record, one letter per month from January. Its records are summarised month by month: value_count lists each month at least one record marks, in calendar order, with the number of records marking it ("Sep (2); Oct (5); Nov (5)"), so the months listed are those any record gives; value_mode is a twelve-letter string marking the months at least half the records give, and method is "majority". A trait is treated so when its definition's type is monthly_presence, or when every one of its records is such a string (as in releases whose definitions call these traits categorical).

Taxa. With collapse_to_species = TRUE, records of a subspecies, variety or form are counted towards their species: the name up to its rank marker (subsp., var., f.), so that Mentha x piperita var. citrata becomes Mentha x piperita. Hybrid formulae and intergrades, such as Acacia trachycarpa x Acacia tumida var. pilbarensis, belong to neither parent and keep their own rows, as do genus-level names. Names without a rank marker, as in zoological trinomials, are not collapsed.

Groups. by splits each taxon's records further, giving one row per taxon, group and trait: by a column of the traits table, such as "life_stage", or, given the database, by a context property, such as "sex" in a database that records it as a context. Records without a value for a by variable form a group of their own (NA).

How much evidence. n_records, n_datasets, n_locations, n_flora and n_field count what is behind each value, and sd_log is the spread of the records on the log scale (empty for a signed trait). reliability is a provisional class from those counts: high with at least 3 datasets and 10 records, medium with at least 2 datasets or 5 records, low otherwise.

The observed mean does not adjust for where in a taxon's range, or under what conditions, its records were collected.

See also

trait_means_dictionary() for the columns; extract_data(), extract_taxa() and extract_trait() to subset a database first.

Examples

means <- summarise_trait_means(austraits_lite, traits = c("leaf_length", "leaf_phenology"))
means
#> # A tibble: 6,852 × 27
#>    taxon_name         trait_name     unit  estimate_type method  value log_value
#>    <chr>              <chr>          <chr> <chr>         <chr>   <dbl>     <dbl>
#>  1 Abroma molle       leaf_length    mm    observed_mean geomet… 122.       4.81
#>  2 Abroma molle       leaf_phenology NA    observed_mean mode     NA       NA   
#>  3 Abrophyllum ornans leaf_length    mm    observed_mean geomet…  99.5      4.60
#>  4 Abrophyllum ornans leaf_phenology NA    observed_mean mode     NA       NA   
#>  5 Abrus precatorius  leaf_length    mm    observed_mean geomet…  11.2      2.41
#>  6 Abrus precatorius  leaf_phenology NA    observed_mean mode     NA       NA   
#>  7 Abutilon auritum   leaf_length    mm    observed_mean geomet…  59.2      4.08
#>  8 Abutilon auritum   leaf_phenology NA    observed_mean mode     NA       NA   
#>  9 Abutilon hannii    leaf_length    mm    observed_mean geomet…  54.8      4.00
#> 10 Abutilon hannii    leaf_phenology NA    observed_mean mode     NA       NA   
#> # ℹ 6,842 more rows
#> # ℹ 20 more variables: arithmetic_mean <dbl>, value_min <dbl>, value_max <dbl>,
#> #   n_records <int>, n_locations <int>, n_datasets <int>, n_flora <int>,
#> #   n_field <int>, sd_log <dbl>, reliability <chr>, dataset_id <chr>,
#> #   source_id <chr>, type <chr>, value_mode <chr>, value_count <chr>,
#> #   taxon_rank <chr>, genus <chr>, family <chr>, establishment_means <chr>,
#> #   taxon_id <chr>

# One genus, split by life stage
austraits_lite |>
  extract_taxa(genus = "Acacia") |>
  summarise_trait_means(traits = "leaf_length", by = "life_stage")
